lead: Today’s readings are joined by one verb: to lift up. Moses lifts a bronze serpent on a pole, and those who look at it live. Jesus says that when the Son of Man is lifted up, people will know who he is. As the Cross comes nearer, the Church sets beside it an old story about complaint, poison and healing. The key words are look, lifted up and I am.

set: Israel is near the end of the desert years. Edom has refused them passage (20:14–21), so they must go the long way around it. Aaron has just died on Mount Hor (20:22–29). The people have been through this complaint before, but here they reject the food God himself has given. “This miserable food” is the manna.
str: vv. 4–5: impatience, and the complaint against God and Moses.
v. 7: the people admit their sin and ask Moses to pray.
vv. 8–9: the remedy: look and live.
¶ Notice that God does not take the serpents away. He gives a way to live though bitten.
kw: The Hebrew calls these “fiery” serpents, perhaps from the burning of the bite, and the NRSV translates “poisonous”. The word has the same root as the seraphim of Isaiah 6.
A play on sound: Moses makes a nĕḥaš nĕḥōšet, a “serpent of bronze”.
Also a banner or signal raised for all to see. The remedy is put where anyone can find it.
vv: and we detest this miserable food.
The bread from heaven has become, for them, something to despise. Complaint can blind us to the gift in our hands.
We have sinned by speaking against the Lord and against you; pray to the Lord to take away the serpents from us.
The first honest word in the passage. Those who spoke against Moses now ask for his prayer, and “Moses prayed for the people” without a word of reproach.
and whenever a serpent bit someone, that person would look at the serpent of bronze and live.
What had brought death is now the shape of healing. Those who were bitten must look at the very thing they fear.
ch: The Book of Wisdom already guards against any magical reading: the one who looked “was saved, not by the thing that was beheld, but by you, the Savior of all” (Wisdom 16:7). And when people later burned incense to the serpent, King Hezekiah broke it in pieces (2 Kings 18:4). The Catechism cites it among the images God allowed that pointed toward salvation through the incarnate Word (CCC 2130). St Justin Martyr makes a similar point in his Dialogue with Trypho, reading it as a sign of the Cross (in substance). Jesus himself draws the line: “just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3:14), and the Church reads Numbers 21 at Mass on the feast of the Exaltation of the Cross.

r.h: When you have lifted up the Son of Man
set: The setting is still the Temple, at the festival of Booths; Jesus has been teaching “in the treasury of the temple” (8:20). He speaks of going away, and the listeners cannot follow his meaning. They wonder if he plans to take his own life, when in fact others are planning his death.
In John, “the Jews” often means the authorities who oppose Jesus, not a whole people; Jesus, his mother and his first disciples were Jews, and many in this very scene believe in him (8:30).
str: vv. 21–22: “I am going away”, and the misunderstanding.
vv. 23–24: from below, from above; “unless you believe”.
vv. 28–29: the Cross will show who he is.
kw: The Greek has no “he”. The words can be an ordinary “It is I”, but in these verses they echo God’s own speech in the Greek Old Testament: “that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he” (Isaiah 43:10; compare Exodus 3:14).
John uses it three times of the Cross (3:14; 8:28; 12:32). It means both raising on a cross and exalting in honor. In this Gospel the two happen together.
vv: for you will die in your sins unless you believe that I am he.
This is a warning, not a verdict. Faith is held out as the way of escape from the very thing he warns of.
Why do I speak to you at all?

A note on the text. The Greek of this reply is famously hard, and translators differ. The NRSV hears a sigh. The Malayalam POC, like the Latin tradition, takes it as “what I have told you from the beginning”. Either way, Jesus does not give them a new title; he points them back to what they have already heard.
When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he,
The Cross will not hide who Jesus is. It will show it. What looks like his defeat is the place where he is known (compare 12:32).
for I always do what is pleasing to him.
He is not alone, even at the hour when all will leave him. Compare 16:32.
ch: The Catechism quotes John 8:28 to teach that the Resurrection confirms the truth of Jesus’ divinity (CCC 653). The Church teaches that Jesus’ death cannot be charged against all the Jews then alive, or against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). Every sinner has a part in it (CCC 598). We read “you have lifted up” as spoken to ourselves.

study: What do I complain about that was first given to me as a gift? What would it mean to give thanks for it today?
When I look at a crucifix, what do I see? What wound of mine can I bring to that look?
